newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Franco-Belgian ties plumb new depths over Renault.
newsitem.headline: Franco-Belgian ties plumb new depths over Renault.

text.p: Franco-Belgian relations, more often than not a case of disdain meets schizophrenia, have plumbed new depths with the sudden announcement last Thursday of the closure of French carmaker Renault's Belgian plant.

The Belgian government is taking Renault to court over the manner in which it announced the closure of what, to make matters worse, is a profitable car plant in Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene's home town.
"The government is indignant and stupefied," Dehaene said after news of the closure. "This decision is unacceptable."
On Tuesday the daily La Derniere Heure summed up the national mood and suggested a strategic retaliation.
"There is only one answer to the financial terrorism of Renault's state shareholder: boycott!", it said.
Dehaene has appealed personally to his French counterpart Alain Juppe to intervene and reverse the closure decision but, to date, Renault is standing by its decision.

It is not the first time France and Belgium have come to diplomatic blows, but in this case it is aggravated by the fact the plant is in the Dutch-speaking Flemish area of the country which has never shaken off its fear and loathing of the French.

French is the language of the southern Walloon region of Belgium which used to run the country, but which is now a poor industrial wasteland in which some are increasingly looking to France for protection from their rich northern cousins.

At the same time, French justice authorities are proving reluctant to cooperate with their Belgian counterparts trying to investigate allegations that French aerospace firm Dassault paid bribes to Belgian political parties for contracts in the 1980s.
Dassault has denied the allegations but Belgium has issued an international arrest warrant for company chief Serge Dassault who risks arrest if he sets foot outside France.
Belgian Justice Minister Stefaan De Clerck has personally asked for better cooperation from France, and Dehaene has said he too will step in unless matters improve.
The affair -- and the unrelated but contemporaneous bribery scandal involving Italian helicopter firm Agusta -- has already ended the careers of some senior Belgian politicians.
It has also turned the Francophone socialist party, a member of the ruling coalition, into what one government source recently termed "a virtual party".

Dassault's reluctance to visit Belgium follows the arrest of fellow countryman Didier Pineau-Valencienne when he voluntarily turned up for questioning in 1994 over alleged fraud when his firm, Schneider, took over some assets in Belgium.

The diplomatic uproar over this arrest cooled when Pineau-Valencienne was freed after 12 days and allowed to return to France. But it boiled again when he later refused to come back, resulting in the issue of an international arrest warrant.
The matter was only sorted out in early 1995 when he struck a deal with the Belgian authorities to come back to give more evidence on the understanding he would not be touched.
Industrio-political rows are not the only ones to buffet the rocky Franco-Belgian relationship.
France was incensed when Belgium, despite intense lobbying to at least stay neutral, joined in the international condemnation of its resumed South Pacific nuclear tests in 1995.
It is a feeling of betrayal that President Jacques Chirac, who had used the tests to stamp his personality on his new presidency, will be slow to forget.

France and Belgium have also clashed over their mutual border which, under the Schengen agreement, is supposed to be completely open but on which France reimposed checks in a bid to stem the flow of drugs it says originates in the Netherlands.
The checks were reinforced when the Algerian fundamentalist bombing campaign began, but the Belgians remain deeply unhappy at what they see as the cavalier attitude of their Big Brother neighbour.

All this is happening at a time when France and Belgium are bidding to be the first to leap into the European Union's single currency bed and are negotiating a common European justice area to enhance cross-border judicial cooperation.
